title: Nicotine dependence · CHRNA5
summary: CHRNA5 makes part of the brain receptor that nicotine binds to. rs16969968 changes Asp398 to Asn. It is one of the most repeated findings in addiction genetics. Among smokers, each A copy is linked to about one more cigarette per day. It is also linked to higher odds of heavy smoking and nicotine dependence: a small shift.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, the reference genotype. In large studies, smokers with this genotype smoke slightly fewer cigarettes per day on average and have lower odds of nicotine dependence than A-allele carriers. This locus says nothing about whether someone smokes at all — social environment and choice dominate that.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A (Asn398) allele. Among people who smoke, this genotype is associated on average with slightly heavier smoking and modestly higher odds of nicotine dependence per A allele: a small shift. It is one small factor among many; it has no meaning for people who never smoke.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A (Asn398) allele. Among smokers, this genotype is linked to the heaviest average cigarette use at this site. It also has higher odds of nicotine dependence than GG: a moderate shift. The effect is an average across large groups. Many AA people never smoke, or quit without trouble.

citations.label: Saccone et al., Hum Mol Genet 2007

title: Alcohol dependence protection · ALDH2
summary: ALDH2 clears acetaldehyde, a toxic product made when the body breaks down alcohol. The A copy at rs671, called ALDH2*2, is common in East Asian groups. It leaves the enzyme mostly inactive and can cause flushing after drinking. Because alcohol then feels unpleasant, A is strongly linked to less heavy drinking and alcohol dependence. This is one of the clearest known links between a gene and behavior.

interpretations.GG: Plain summary: no flush variant here — this gene does not change your alcohol-related risks either way, and the usual guidance on drinking still applies. Two working copies of ALDH2. Acetaldehyde is cleared normally, no genetic flushing reaction, and no protection against heavy drinking from this locus. Drinking patterns for this genotype are shaped by culture, environment, and other genes.
interpretations.AG: Plain summary: This risk does not apply if little or no alcohol is used. Heavy drinking with this DNA type raises the risk of throat cancer. AG has one inactive ALDH2*2 copy and occurs mainly in people with East Asian ancestry. Acetaldehyde builds up after alcohol and often causes a red face and nausea. AG is linked to far less alcohol dependence. People who drink heavily despite flushing have a higher risk of esophageal cancer in population studies. The flush should be taken seriously.
interpretations.AA: Plain summary: Alcohol usually feels very unpleasant with AA. No extra risk applies if little or no alcohol is used. Heavy drinking despite flushing brings the highest acetaldehyde-related throat-cancer risk. AA has two inactive ALDH2*2 copies. Even small amounts of alcohol often cause strong flushing. Alcohol dependence is rare because drinking is so unpleasant. This is a common group pattern, not a rule for one person.

title: Alcohol dependence protection · ADH1B
summary: ADH1B turns alcohol into acetaldehyde. The T copy at rs1229984 is His48, also called ADH1B*2. It makes the enzyme work faster: a large shift, not a small one. The quick acetaldehyde rise can make drinking less pleasant. Across many groups, T carriers have much lower rates of alcohol dependence. A large review found one of the strongest single-gene protective links in addiction genetics. This site has more than two forms; this report covers common T and C.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies make the slower Arg48 form. This is the common form in European and African groups. Alcohol is broken down at the usual rate. CC gives no protection from heavy drinking at this site. Life context and other genes matter far more.
interpretations.CT: One T copy makes the fast His48 form. Alcohol turns into acetaldehyde more quickly. Many carriers feel mild unpleasant effects after drinking. Large reviews link CT to much lower odds of alcohol dependence than CC. This is a group-level protective link, not a sure result for one person.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies make the fast His48 form. TT is the most common type in East Asian groups and is uncommon in European groups. Alcohol turns into acetaldehyde very quickly. TT has the lowest average rate of alcohol dependence at this site. Heavy drinking is still possible and has its usual harms.

title: Response to opioid medicines · OPRM1
summary: OPRM1 makes the mu-opioid receptor. Opioid pain medicines and endorphins act mainly through this receptor. The G copy at rs1799971 changes Asn40 to Asp. A large joint review linked G to slightly lower overall likelihood of substance dependence. Some clinical studies link it to needing a little more opioid medicine for the same pain relief. Effects are small, and results for specific addictions do not agree.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A (Asn40) allele, the most common genotype worldwide. Mu-opioid receptor function is the reference baseline, and opioid medication dosing studies use this group as the comparison. This genotype carries no particular signal in either direction at this locus.
interpretations.AG: One G copy makes the Asp40 form. Studies link G carriers to slightly different feelings from alcohol and opioids. Some surgery studies also link G to a need for slightly more opioid medicine. The largest review found slightly lower overall substance-dependence likelihood. Each effect is small, and many other factors matter.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies make the Asp40 form. GG is most common in East Asian groups. It shows the strongest version of the small G pattern in group studies. These include changed opioid response in pain studies and slightly lower substance-dependence likelihood. Medicine response still varies widely for other reasons. This result is information, not a dosing guide.

title: Brain reward signaling · ANKK1/DRD2 Taq1A
summary: The Taq1A variant (rs1800497) sits in ANKK1, next to the dopamine D2 receptor gene DRD2. The A allele was once called “A1”. Brain imaging links it to fewer available D2 receptors. In meta-analyses it is linked to modestly higher odds of alcohol dependence: a small shift. It is one of the oldest findings in addiction genetics. But the literature shows publication bias, and the true effect is likely small.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G ('A2') allele, the most common genotype in most populations. Striatal dopamine D2 receptor availability is at the reference baseline on average, and this genotype is the comparison group in addiction association studies at this locus.
interpretations.AG: One A copy, once called A1, occurs in about one third of people with European ancestry. Brain scans link A to somewhat fewer D2 receptors on average. Reviews link it to higher odds of alcohol dependence: a small shift. This is a weak group link. It is one small factor among hundreds of gene and life effects on reward and habit.
interpretations.AA: Two A ('A1') alleles, a less common genotype. Associated on average with the lowest D2 receptor availability at this locus and, in meta-analyses, slightly elevated odds of alcohol and other substance dependence. The effect size is small and studies conflict; most people with this genotype never develop any substance problem.

title: Cannabinoid response · CNR1
summary: CNR1 makes the CB1 receptor, the main brain target of THC. In small studies of cannabis users, people with C at rs2023239 reported more craving and withdrawal while not using cannabis. Their reward brain regions also responded differently to cannabis cues. The study groups were small, and later results have not been steady. This is an early and uncertain link.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, the most common genotype. In the small studies done so far, this group reported comparatively lower cannabis craving and withdrawal during abstinence. Evidence at this locus is preliminary, and cannabis-use outcomes depend overwhelmingly on non-genetic factors.
interpretations.CT: One C allele, present in roughly a third of people of European ancestry. Small studies associate C-allele carriers who use cannabis with greater average craving and withdrawal during abstinence and stronger neural responses to cannabis cues. These are preliminary findings from limited samples — one small and uncertain factor.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies form an uncommon type. If the early link is real, CC may follow the C-carrier pattern. That means more craving and withdrawal on average among cannabis users. No study has included enough people to describe CC on its own. This result needs great caution.

title: Habitual caffeine intake · AHR
summary: AHR controls CYP1A2, a liver enzyme that clears most caffeine. Studies of hundreds of thousands of people link C at rs4410790 to slightly more coffee use. Each C copy adds about one tenth of a cup per day on average. Faster caffeine clearance may lead to more frequent use. The link repeats well but is tiny.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele. Associated on average with slightly lower habitual coffee and caffeine consumption than C carriers — a difference of a fraction of a cup a day at the population level. Personal preference, sleep habits, and culture matter far more.
interpretations.CT: One C copy gives a middle result at this site. On average, CT is linked to slightly more daily caffeine than TT. A small rise in caffeine clearance may explain the link. The effect appears in large groups but is tiny for one person.
interpretations.CC: Two C alleles. Associated with the highest average habitual coffee and caffeine intake at this locus — still only around a quarter of a cup per day more than TT on average. This describes consumption patterns, not caffeine's health effects.

citations.label: Sulem et al., Hum Mol Genet 2011

title: Alcohol consumption · KLB
summary: KLB makes beta-Klotho, part of a liver-to-brain hormone receptor. Through this receptor, FGF21 lowers alcohol preference in animal studies. A study of more than 100,000 people linked G at rs11940694 to slightly more alcohol each week. Later biobank studies found the link again. Each G copy changes weekly drinks by very little.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele. Associated on average with slightly lower weekly alcohol consumption than G carriers in large population studies. The difference is a statistical shift of a fraction of a drink per week — habits, environment, and choice dominate actual intake.
interpretations.AG: One G allele — about half of people carry this genotype. Associated with an intermediate, very small average increase in weekly alcohol consumption relative to AA. This locus relates to typical consumption in drinkers, not to dependence, and is one tiny factor among many.
interpretations.GG: Two G alleles. Associated with the highest average weekly alcohol consumption at this locus, though the absolute difference from AA is small at the individual level. Population averages at a single variant say little about any one person's drinking.

title: Endocannabinoid breakdown · FAAH
summary: FAAH breaks down anandamide, a cannabinoid made by the brain. The A copy at rs324420 changes Pro129 to Thr. It makes the enzyme less stable and raises anandamide levels. The first study linked AA to more problem street-drug use. Later work links A to small differences in stress response and cannabis effects. Other studies did not always agree, so this is an early link.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Pro129) allele, the most common genotype. FAAH enzyme stability is at the reference baseline, and this group serves as the comparison in association studies. No particular signal at this locus.
interpretations.AC: One A (Thr129) allele. FAAH activity is modestly reduced on average, which raises baseline anandamide signaling. Studies associate A carriers with subtle differences in stress and reward responses; links to substance-use problems are inconsistent across cohorts. A preliminary, small factor at most.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies make the uncommon Thr129 type. AA greatly lowers FAAH stability. A 2002 study found AA more often among people who reported problem street-drug use. Later studies did not always find the same result. This is an early, uncertain group link and cannot predict one person.

title: Smoking initiation · BDNF
summary: The Tobacco and Genetics Consortium studied more than 70,000 people. Its review found a broad-study signal for the BDNF Val66Met change, rs6265. The common C/Val copy was linked to slightly higher odds of ever smoking often: a very small shift. The effect is tiny. Social setting, time period, and other life factors matter far more to whether someone starts smoking.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (Val) allele. Associated in large meta-analyses with very slightly higher odds of ever taking up regular smoking per C allele: a very small shift. This is a barely-detectable statistical tilt found only in huge samples — one small factor, dwarfed by social environment.
interpretations.CT: One C/Val and one T/Met copy give a middle result at this site. The average difference in smoking-start odds is very small. This type has almost no power to predict one person's smoking behavior.
interpretations.TT: Two T (Met) alleles, an uncommon genotype in most populations. Associated on average with slightly lower odds of ever becoming a regular smoker. As with the other genotypes here, the effect is tiny and only visible when averaging across tens of thousands of people.

citations.label: Tobacco and Genetics Consortium, Nat Genet 2010
